Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Vignette:
Somchai was 60 and had spent most of his life at sea, rising before dawn to work as a fisherman along the South Eastern Asian coast after settling in the United States with his wife. He was a man used to weather, engines, and the hard routines of the water, but the event that changed him had nothing to do with a storm. Several years earlier, while he was at work on another boat, he had received word that a close relative had been caught in a violent accident onshore and did not survive. By the time Somchai reached the hospital, the person he had rushed to see was already gone. What stayed with him most was not only the loss itself, but the helplessness of arriving too late, standing among strangers, and seeing the grief of the family gathered around the bed. He replayed that day often, especially the moment he had been told the news and the long, silent drive afterward when he could not think of anything except that one life had ended while his had continued.

In the weeks that followed, Somchai found that reminders could strike him with startling force. The sound of an ambulance passing near the docks could make his chest tighten and his body jerk into a state of alarm, as if something terrible were happening again. Even the sight of a hospital parking lot while driving his wife to an appointment could leave him suddenly nauseated and tense, his heart pounding so strongly that he would grip the steering wheel until his hands ached. At times he was overwhelmed by fear, anger, and guilt in quick succession, and he described these feelings as coming over him before he could organize them into words. At night, he lay awake long after his wife had fallen asleep, listening to the ceiling fan and worrying that he would never truly rest. Other nights he would doze only briefly before waking again, already alert, his mind returning to that phone call and the sickening knowledge that he had not been there in time.

Over the months, Somchai began to move through his days with a strange kind of distance. He continued to fish, but he did so with less ease, keeping to himself on the boat and speaking less than he once had. His wife noticed that he responded to sad news in a flat, almost distant way, as though he had become “dead inside,” his own phrase for the numbness that frightened him most. He no longer took comfort in the things that used to steady him, and when he sat at home after work he seemed to stare through the room rather than into it. What troubled him was that he could not restore the old sense of trust he once had in other people. If someone said they would call, he wondered whether they truly would; if a neighbor offered help, he suspected there might be something unspoken behind it. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted fully, because life could change without warning and because promises had not spared his loved one from dying. That mistrust showed itself in everyday interactions, including at the docks, where he became more guarded with other fishermen and less willing to depend on them for small favors or shared plans.

The loss also carried a weight of guilt that Somchai rarely voiced aloud. He wondered why he had survived and his loved one had not, and the question stayed with him in quiet moments, especially when he was alone on the water and the sea was still. He felt he should have been closer, faster, somehow able to prevent what happened. Instead, he had lived through the day and returned to work, while others had not. That thought made his grief feel unjust and personal, as though survival itself were a kind of betrayal. Over time, his wife saw him withdrawing from family gatherings and becoming harder to reach emotionally, but he did not describe it as withdrawal; he said only that he felt emptied out.

By the time he sought help, Somchai had grown tired of living with the same tight surge in his body whenever something reminded him of that day, the same sleepless nights, and the same persistent conviction that trust was fragile and survival carried a debt. He came in after realizing how often he was bracing for bad news and how little relief he felt even on ordinary days. What he most feared was that he would go on feeling this way indefinitely, unable to sleep, unable to feel fully present with his wife, and unable to stop the guilt that returned whenever he remembered who had died and who had lived.
